sections.title: Ground Anchors
sections.summary: A prestressed grouted ground anchor is a structural element that transmits tensile load into the ground via grout. Components: (1) anchorage (head + bearing plate + trumpet); (2) unbonded length (free to elongate, bondbreaker sleeve prevents grout bond); (3) tendon bond length (bonded to grout, transfers load). Four types: Type A — straight shaft gravity-grouted (rock and very stiff/hard clay); Type B — straight shaft pressure-grouted (coarse granular and fissured rock, grout >0.35 MPa); Type C — post-grouted (multiple injections to enlarge grout body); Type D — underreamed (firm/hard cohesive soil, end-bearing supplement). Grout: w/c = 0.4–0.55, min 21 MPa at stressing.
sections.body:
A prestressed grouted ground anchor transmits an applied tensile load into the ground through a cement-grouted drill hole. The anchor consists of: (1) anchorage — anchor head + bearing plate + trumpet at the wall face; (2) free stressing (unbonded) length — allows elastic elongation; protected by smooth bondbreaker sleeve; (3) tendon bond length — bonded to grout, located behind the critical failure surface. The anchor bond length is the portion of the drill hole that is grouted and transfers load to the ground.

The tendon includes prestressing steel, corrosion protection, sheaths, centralizers, and spacers, but excludes the grout. A sheath is a smooth or corrugated tube that protects the unbonded length from corrosion. Centralizers position the tendon to provide minimum grout cover. Spacers separate multiple strands or bars to ensure individual bonding to grout.

Four main anchor types: Type A — straight shaft gravity-grouted (tremie method) for rock and very stiff to hard cohesive soils. Type B — straight shaft pressure-grouted; grout injected at >0.35 MPa for coarse granular soils and weak fissured rock; increases normal stress and effective diameter of grout bulb. Type C — post-grouted; multiple delayed injections via check-valve tubes enlarge the gravity-grouted anchor body; most complex but highest capacity. Type D — underreamed (series of bells), used in firm to hard cohesive soils; mobilizes end-bearing in addition to side shear.

Tendon materials: Bar tendons per ASTM A722 — diameters 26, 32, 36, 45, 64 mm; uncoupled lengths up to ~18 m; max design load ~2,077 kN for 64 mm bar; adjustable load after lock-off. Strand tendons per ASTM A416 — 15 mm diameter seven-wire strand, multiple strands, no practical length limit; lower relaxation properties. Epoxy-coated bars (AASHTO M284) and epoxy-coated filled strand (per ASTM A882 supplement) provide additional corrosion protection. Indented strand per ASTM A886.

Cement grout: neat cement grout per ASTM C150; w/c = 0.4 to 0.55; Type I cement; min 21 MPa compressive strength at anchor stressing. Sand-cement grout acceptable for large diameter drill holes. Plasticizers may be used for high-temperature or long-distance pumping applications.
key_points: Ground anchor components: anchorage (head/plate/trumpet), unbonded length (bondbreaker sleeve), tendon bond length
Type A: gravity-grouted (rock/stiff clay); Type B: pressure-grouted >0.35 MPa (granular/fissured rock)
Type C: post-grouted (multiple injections via check valves); Type D: underreamed (end-bearing in stiff clay)
Bar tendons: ASTM A722, 26–64 mm dia., up to 18 m uncoupled; strand: ASTM A416, 15 mm, no length limit
Grout: w/c = 0.4–0.55, Type I Portland cement; min 21 MPa at stressing per ASTM C150

sections.title: Anchored Walls
sections.summary: The most common anchored wall in the U.S. is the soldier beam and lagging wall — discrete steel soldier beams at 1.5–3 m spacing spanned by timber (or shotcrete) lagging, with one or more levels of ground anchors. Drilled-in soldier beams use lean-mix concrete (min 0.35 MPa) below excavation subgrade and lean-mix above (to allow scraping). Construction sequence: top-down in 1.2–1.5 m lifts; halt excavation 0.6 m below anchor level, install and test anchor, lock-off, then continue. Continuous wall systems (sheet piles, slurry walls, secant pile walls) do not require lagging and are commonly used for temporary SOE.
sections.body:
Soldier beam and lagging walls are the most commonly used anchored wall type in the U.S. Horizontal soldier beam spacing typically varies from 1.5 to 3 m. Steel beams (WF or HP shapes) may be driven or drilled-in. Drilled-in soldier beams are placed in excavated holes backfilled with structural concrete from the bottom to the excavation subgrade, then lean-mix concrete (1 bag Portland cement per cubic yard; max ~1 MPa) from subgrade to grade. Lean-mix concrete is scraped off during lagging installation. CLSM (flowable fill with cement, fine aggregate, and fly ash) may substitute for lean-mix concrete; min 0.35 MPa required. Driven soldier beams use HP shapes or steel sheet piles; connected to anchors via thru-beam connections (for small diameter anchors) or horizontal wales.

Lagging: Excavation in 1.2–1.5 m lifts (smaller in cohesionless or soft ground with limited stand-up time). Lagging installed from top-down immediately after excavation. Timber or reinforced shotcrete lagging placed between or in front of soldier beam flanges. Gaps between vertically adjacent lagging boards accommodate drainage ('louvers'). Concrete lagging has been used but is difficult to trim and may crack during anchor testing.

Construction sequence (soldier beam and lagging): (1) Install soldier beams; (2) Excavate and install lagging top-down; (3) When excavation reaches 0.6 m below anchor level, halt excavation; (4) Install, test, and lock-off ground anchor; (5) Continue excavation to next anchor level or final depth; (6) After reaching final depth, install drainage, permanent concrete facing.

Continuous walls (sheet-pile, slurry walls, tangent/secant pile): Act as both vertical and horizontal wall elements. Sheet-pile walls driven in one phase. Continuous walls must address water pressure (watertight connection at anchor/wall interface needed for hydrostatic conditions).
key_points: Soldier beam and lagging: most common U.S. type; soldier beam spacing 1.5–3 m; timber lagging excavated top-down in 1.2–1.5 m lifts
Drilled-in soldier beam backfill: structural concrete below subgrade; lean-mix (min 0.35 MPa) above for easy scraping
Halt excavation 0.6 m below anchor elevation; install, test, and lock-off anchor before continuing
Lagging boards require 'louver' gaps for drainage between vertically adjacent boards
Continuous walls (sheet-pile, slurry, secant): no lagging required; water pressure must be addressed explicitly

sections.title: Applications of Ground Anchors
sections.summary: Ground anchors are used in three main highway applications: (1) retaining walls for grade separations (depressed roadways, widenings, realignments, bridge abutments) — advantages over gravity walls include no select backfill, no temporary support, and eliminated deep foundations; (2) slope and landslide stabilization — anchors combined with walls, horizontal beams, or concrete blocks to resist sliding mass forces, which may be larger than typical retaining wall forces; (3) tiedown structures — resist vertical uplift from hydrostatic or overturning forces in underwater or subterranean applications.
sections.body:
Highway retaining walls: Anchored walls are used for grade separations to construct depressed roadways, widenings, and realignments. Compared to concrete gravity walls, permanent anchored walls eliminate the need for: temporary excavation support; select backfill; and deep foundation support. Construction time and ROW acquisition are also reduced. Applications include new bridge abutment construction and end slope removal for existing bridge abutments.

Slope and landslide stabilization: Ground anchors are used in combination with walls, horizontal beams, or concrete blocks to stabilize slopes and landslides. The required stabilization force may be considerably greater than that for a typical highway retaining wall. Horizontal beams or concrete blocks transfer anchor loads to the slope surface. Cost, aesthetics, and long-term maintenance affect the selection of surface connection system.

Tiedown structures: Permanent ground anchors resist vertical uplift forces from hydrostatic or overturning loads. Used where a structure has insufficient dead weight to counteract uplift. Advantages: reduced concrete volume in slabs; reduced excavation/dewatering. Disadvantages: large load variations from settlement and heave; difficulty of watertight anchor-slab connections; stress variations in slab. Rock anchor tiedowns are also used to stabilize concrete dams (overturning, sliding, earthquake resistance).
key_points: Retaining walls: eliminates temporary support, select backfill, and deep foundations for highway cut walls
Slope stabilization: stabilization force may be much greater than typical wall loads; use with horizontal beams or concrete blocks
Tiedowns: resist hydrostatic or overturning uplift; challenges include load variation with GWT change and watertight connections
